title: Should We Please and Thank Students?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a former professor's advice never to say please or thank you to students, Stuart interrogates his own classroom language and discovers he genuinely doesn't use those words with students, then works out why. His argument is that please and thank you aren't the only vehicles for signaling respect for a student's autonomy and appreciation for their cooperation; a teacher can convey the same substance through tone, specific praise, and directive language without the transactional politeness formula. He walks through the phrases he substitutes in practice, framed as part of cultivating what he calls a warmly authoritative teacher presence. He's careful to frame this as a rule of thumb rather than a rigid rule, and invites disagreement, but lands on cautious agreement with the provocative advice that started the piece.
points: Stuart's claim is that omitting please and thank you isn't coldness; it's a deliberate substitution of substance (respect, appreciation) for the ritual words that can otherwise imply compliance is optional.
He offers concrete swap-in language ("let's begin," "that was well done") that models what warmly authoritative instruction sounds like without the please/thank-you formula.
He frames the practice as an exercise in developing "warmly authoritative teacher presence" rather than a moral rule, explicitly declining to be doctrinaire about it.
quotes: One of my professors, towards the beginning of my program, told my cohort that we shouldn't use please or thank you when talking to students. The reasoning was that if we are asking or thanking a student for meeting classroom expectations, that using those words suggests to them that their behavior wasn't necessary or required of them.
But then I started thinking about what I actually say with my students. Are there times when I say please and thank you to them? And, to my surprise, I found that my answer was no.

Please and thank you aren't the only ways to communicate to human beings that you recognize their right to refuse cooperation, and that you appreciate them cooperating. And so it's possible to express these things without saying them outright.
It's not that I never say these things, I don't have any rules like that. But weirdly, I do kind of agree with the professor here.

I think it's a good rule of thumb to remove these words from your vocabulary a bit so that you can get used to speaking like a warmly authoritative teacher. It's nothing to be religious about, certainly. But it is a helpful thought.
